title: Measuring the Security of the Evolving Software Supply Chain: a Research Agenda

numericClaims.quote: Supply chain attacks have demonstrated that the compromise of a single dependency or maintainer can have widespread consequences across thousands of downstream applications.
RQ4: How have dependency patterns evolved across software ecosystems following the adoption of LLM-assisted software development compared to the pre-LLM era?

The study by Zahan et al. [3] also reported several supply chain attack vectors, including install scripts, unmaintained packages, and expired domains, arising from maintainers being overloaded with a large number of packages.

Taken together, these studies converge on two key structural patterns in software ecosystems: i) popular packages have a high-impact attack surface, as several libraries depend on them, and ii) a small number of highly influential maintainers affect a large portion of the ecosystem.

Zhao et al. [1] investigated the effectiveness of SCA tools in the Java Maven ecosystem by proposing a new evaluation model that considers execution environments, dependency and vulnerability detection mechanisms, and dependency selection.

Similarly, Okafor et al. [15] introduced three key security principles combining dependency transparency, component validity, and the separation of development stages to support ecosystem-wide analysis.

To address the lack of standardization in dependency graph construction, Litzenberger et al. [18] proposed the Dependency Graph Mining Framework (DGMF) as a unified solution for building dependency graphs from different software repositories.

questions.question: How many research questions does the paper formulate, and what label range do they span?
questions.answer: Five research questions, labeled RQ0 through RQ4: state of the art in measuring/modeling supply chain security (RQ0), a unified measurement model for dependency graphs and vulnerability exposure (RQ1), source code-level reachability analysis to reduce alert fatigue (RQ2), LLM-generated code introducing new dependencies (RQ3), and evolution of dependency patterns after LLM-assisted development vs. the pre-LLM era (RQ4).

questions.question: Which bibliometric analysis tools were used to construct and visualize the citation graphs in the literature review?
questions.answer: VOSviewer and CiteNet Explorer; the graph shown in Figure 2 was generated with VOSviewer.

questions.question: Which two dependency-security metrics did Rahman et al. introduce, and what do they mean?
questions.answer: MTTRdep (Mean Time To Remediate dependencies: average time required to remediate vulnerable dependencies) and MTTUdep (Mean Time To Update dependencies: average time required to update dependencies).

questions.question: What tool did Alfadel et al. develop for the PyPI ecosystem, and which ecosystem did they compare PyPI against?
questions.answer: DEPHEALTH, a tool designed to detect and report vulnerabilities; the PyPI ecosystem was studied in comparison with npm.

questions.question: Which vulnerability type was most common in the cross-ecosystem studies of PyPI/npm and RubyGems?
questions.answer: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) was the most common vulnerability type, with most discovered vulnerabilities of medium or high severity.

questions.question: What concept did Zhao et al. propose to reduce false positives and false negatives in Maven project analysis?
questions.answer: The Scan Scope Maven (SSM) concept, which reduces both false positives and false negatives by defining the required dependencies to include during project analysis.

questions.question: What is Ranger, introduced by Zhang et al., and what does it do?
questions.answer: A tool that automatically restores version ranges while preserving compatibility with existing code bases, reducing the risk of breaking changes and limiting the persistence of security flaws.

questions.question: What system did Li et al. propose for identifying relevant patch commits, and how does it work?
questions.answer: PatchFinder, which identifies relevant patch commits by leveraging semantic similarity and contextual code understanding, improving the reliability of the results.

questions.question: What are the three main stages of the proposed research methodology?
questions.answer: (1) Literature review and state of the art, (2) the design of a generalized measurement approach, and (3) the investigation of its applicability for improving software supply chain security.

questions.question: From which sources will data be collected in the data-collection and ecosystem-extraction phase?
questions.answer: Package managers (e.g., npm, PyPI, Maven), source code repositories such as GitHub and Bitbucket, and dependency metadata APIs; the collected data includes dependency graphs, version histories, release metadata, and vulnerability reports.

questions.question: Which static analysis engine developed by GitHub does the paper cite as an example of source-code analysis for reachability?
questions.answer: CodeQL, described in a footnote as a static analysis engine developed by GitHub for querying source code as a database.

questions.question: What is the MARIN framework and what does it do?
questions.answer: A framework proposed by Dusing et al. that automates repetitive technical tasks in Maven ecosystem analysis while improving performance through parallel processing.
